Department of Integrative Biological Sciences and Industry, College of Life Sciences, Sejong University Seoul Republic of Korea ([ROR:00aft1q37](https://ror.org/00aft1q37)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract The gram-negative bacterium lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is frequently administered to generate models of systemic inflammation. However, there are several side effects and no effective treatment for LPS-induced systemic inflammation. PEGylated PDZ peptide based on zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) was analyzed for its effects on systemic inflammation induced by LPS. PDZ peptide administration led to the restoration of tissue injuries (kidney, liver, and lung) and prevented alterations in biochemical plasma markers. The production of pro-inflammatory cytokines was significantly decreased in the plasma and lung BALF in the PDZ-administered mice. Flow cytometry analysis revealed the PDZ peptide significantly inhibited inflammation, mainly by decreasing the population of M1 macrophages, and neutrophils (immature and mature), and increasing M2 macrophages. Using RNA sequencing analysis, the expression levels of the NF-κB-related proteins were lower in PDZ-treated cells than in LPS-treated cells. In addition, wild-type PDZ peptide significantly increased mitochondrial membrane integrity and decreased LPS-induced mitochondria fission. Interestingly, PDZ peptide dramatically could reduce LPS-induced NF-κB signaling, ROS production, and the expression of M1 macrophage marker proteins, but increased the expression of M2 macrophage marker proteins. These results indicated that PEGylated PDZ peptide inhibits LPS-induced systemic inflammation, reducing tissue injuries and reestablishing homeostasis, and may be a therapeutic candidate against systemic inflammation. ## Introduction Systemic inflammation causes significant morbidity and mortality worldwide (Juskewitch et al., 2012) and is a common cause of pathogenesis for multiple degenerative diseases, such as cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, autoimmune and neurodegenerative disorders, and coronary heart disease (Qin et al., 2007; Furman et al., 2019; Sattar et al., 2003). One major source of morbidities is pro-inflammatory cytokines from immune cells and activation of the innate immune system against pathogens (Furman et al., 2019). However, the physiological mechanisms and therapeutic candidates against LPS-induced systemic inflammation are poorly understood. ZO-1 is a tight junction protein that regulates cell permeability in many mammalian cells and functions as a scaffolding protein. ZO-1 consists of three PDZ domains, a SH3 domain, and a guanylate kinase (GuK) domain. Because the ZO-1 protein strictly and completely regulates cell permeability, ZO-1 overexpression could inhibit LPS- and PM2.5-induced respiratory inflammation by diminishing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Lee et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2020). Notably, among ZO-1 proteins, PDZ could participate in PDZ-PDZ interactions and bind with non-PDZ-containing proteins (Lee and Zheng, 2010). The PDZ peptide consists of a core sequence that significantly decreases LPS-induced F-actin polymerization and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and/or chemokines to maintain homeostasis (Lee et al., 2020). In addition, RGS12 expression activated by the PDZ peptide can completely block LPS-induced CXCR2 GPCR activation (Lee et al., 2020). Although the PDZ peptide can regulate LPS-and PM2.5-related airway inflammation, this is limited to the respiratory system. The effects of the PDZ peptide on LPS-induced systemic inflammation are poorly understood. M1 and M2 macrophage polarization differs in specific functions in the immune system (Zhang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023). M1 macrophages are the initial immune response to infections and can produce pro-inflammatory cytokines. M2 macrophages are mediated for anti-inflammation and tissue repair and have specific physiological functions to produce anti-inflammatory cytokines and tissue remodeling (Li et al., 2023). Polarization of macrophages into these subtypes is important because it determines the progression to inflammation or anti-inflammation. Neutrophils are a type of white blood cell that mainly assist the body in fighting off infections (Chung et al., 2023). Immature neutrophils can be present but do not participate in infection control, while mature neutrophils are fully functional and primed for fighting infections (Chung et al., 2023). Therefore, the presence of immature neutrophils in the bloodstream may be an indication of inflammation or infection. Here, we suggest that PEGylated PDZ peptide inhibits LPS-induced systemic inflammation by hindering ROS production in the kidney mitochondria. Because the PDZ peptide restored LPS-induced tissue injury in the liver, kidney, and lung in mice, it likely inhibits the major symptoms of systemic inflammation and may be an innovative therapeutic candidate for sepsis and septic shock. ## Results ### ZO-1-based PDZ peptide is generated and PEGylated Based on our previous studies (Lee et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2020), ZO-1 protein potentially regulates LPS- or PM2.5-induced airway inflammation by enforcing membrane tightness. In addition, the PDZ domain plays an essential role in LPS- or PM2.5-induced ZO-1 physiological function by generating TEER. Therefore, we hypothesized that PDZ peptide downregulates systemic LPS inflammation. The PDZ peptide consisting of 22 amino acids and an additional TAT (GRKKRRQRRR) sequence to enable cell permeability was tagged with FITC for monitoring (Figure 1a). The clinical application of a therapeutic peptide is often limited by its short in vivo half-life. PEGylation is one of the well-established approaches for extending in vivo half-life of a peptide drug; A PEGylated peptide is expected to be more tolerable to renal clearance and proteolytic degradation. To PEGylate WT PDZ or mut PDZ at its amine groups, m-PEG-succinimidyl succinate with an average molecular weight of 5000 Da was incubated with WT PDZ or mut PDZ to yield mono- and di-PEGylated WT PDZ or mut PDZ, collectively referred to as PEG-WT-PDZ or PEG-mut PDZ, respectively. Size exclusion chromatography on the PEGylation mixture resulted in the separation of PEG-WT-PDZ or PEG-mut PDZ from unreacted PEG and residual WT PDZ or mut PDZ (Figure 1b). PEG-WT PDZ or PEG-mut PDZ collected from eluting fractions was analyzed by in-gel fluorescence upon SDS-PAGE (Figure 1c). In comparison to the PEGylation mixture which contained native PDZ as well as PEGylated PDZs, purified PEG-WT PDZ or PEG-mut PDZ was comprised of only mono- and di-PEGylates with fairly retarded migration. These results indicated that PEGylation was successfully achieved through amine-coupling at lysine residues of PDZs and substantially increased the hydrodynamic volume of PDZs. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/95285/elife-95285-fig1-v1.jpg) **Figure 1.:** (A) Peptides were synthesized with fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) and entered the Tat region (italicized amino acids) for cell penetration based on the first PDZ domain sequence (A, upper panel), and 25GG26 was changed to 25AA26 for the mutant PDZ peptide (mut PDZ peptide; lower panel). Samples were run on SDS-PAGE and then illuminated at λex  = 480  nm to obtain in-gel fluorescence. ### PDZ peptide exerts anti-inflammatory effects against LPS-induced systemic inflammation in LPS-administered mice We examined the anti-inflammatory effects of the PDZ peptide on LPS-administered mice. Mice were pretreated with either WT or mut PDZ peptide (7.5 mg/kg, i.v.) for 4 hr and then injected with LPS (10 mg/kg, i.p.) to induce experimental systemic inflammation. After sacrifice, blood samples were collected, and the ALT, AST, BUN, and creatinine levels were measured to identify the changes in plasma biochemical markers (Table 1). A significant increase in plasma biomarkers of systemic inflammation was observed in LPS-administered mice. Notably, WT PDZ-treated mice had decreased levels of biomarkers compared to LPS-treated mice. However, mut PDZ-treated mice had not changed, except creatinine, suggesting that WT PDZ peptide significantly decreased LPS-induced elevation of creatinine in plasma. Although the function of ZO-1 protein as a diagnostic marker for sepsis was identified in 2020 year (Ni et al., 2020), additional studies have not been performed. Here, the in vivo survival effect of LPS and PDZ co-administration was examined in mice. The pretreatment with WT PDZ peptide significantly increased survival and rescued compared to LPS only; these effects were not observed with the mut PDZ peptide (Figure 2a). To investigate whether WT PDZ peptide can affect pro-inflammatory cytokine production/recruitment in the plasma after LPS administration, various pre-inflammatory cytokines were measured after blood perfusion through the heart. The IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α levels were significantly decreased in the plasma of WT PDZ peptide-administered mice, but not in mut PDZ peptide-administered mice (Figure 2b). Next, systemic inflammation can cause septic shock and severe damage to lung, kidney, liver, and other organs (Caraballo and Jaimes, 2019; Lelubre and Vincent, 2018). Thus, lung inflammation was examined under the same conditions. The levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines were examined using specific ELISAs (Figure 2c). The LPS-induced pro-inflammatory cytokines production was significantly inhibited in WT PDZ peptide-administered mice, but not in mut PDZ peptide-administered mice. These results indicate that the WT PDZ peptide significantly inhibits the LPS-induced the loss of weight and pro-inflammatory cytokine production to maintain homeostasis in blood and lungs after LPS administration. ![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/95285/elife-95285-fig2-v1.jpg) **Figure 2.:** (A) Comparison of survival rate and body weight change after administration of LPS or both LPS and PDZ peptide. ### PDZ inhibits LPS-induced tissue injury by blocking ROS formation Next, we assessed whether WT PDZ peptide affects acute tissue damage in organs such as the liver, kidney, and lung during LPS-induced systemic inflammation. The liver, kidney, and lung samples were collected and histopathologically examined. LPS administration significantly enhanced inflammatory cell infiltration in the liver (Figure 3a), kidney (Figure 3b), and lung (Figure 3c) tissue samples. Interestingly, these infiltrations were significantly inhibited by WT PDZ administration, but not mut PDZ in the liver, kidney, and lung. And the immunohistochemistry staining using macrophage and microglia marker, Iba1, is helpful for the indication of an inflamed site. Iba1 staining was strongly positive in LPS-administrated Liver and kidney. Interestingly, this iba1 staining was dramatically decreased in WT PDZ treatment, but not mut PDZ in the liver and kidney. In addition, LPS administration increased PAS-positive goblet cells in lung tissue (Figure 3c). PAS-positive goblet cells were strongly decreased by WT PDZ administration, but not by mut PDZ administration. The specific physiological mechanism by which WT PDZ peptide decreases LPS-induced systemic inflammation in mice and the signal molecules involved remain unclear. These were confirmed by a semi-quantitative analysis of Iba-1 immunoreactivity and PAS staining in the liver, kidney, and lung, respectively (Figure 4d, e and f). To examine whether WT PDZ peptide can alter LPS-induced tissue damage in the kidney, a cell toxicity assay was performed (Figure 3g). LPS induced cell damage in the kidney, however, WT PDZ peptide could significantly alleviate the toxicity, but mut PDZ peptide could not. Because cytotoxicity caused by LPS is frequently due to ROS production in the kidney (Su et al., 2023; Qiongyue et al., 2022), ROS production in the mitochondria was investigated in renal mitochondria cells harvested from kidney tissue (Figure 3h). LPS significantly increased ROS production to induce renal inflammation in a time-dependent manner; however, the WT PDZ peptide blocked LPS-induced ROS production, but the mut PDZ peptide did not. All data shown are representative of three independent experiments. ### PDZ peptide regulates LPS-induced immune populations by inhibiting M1 macrophage polarization and promoting M2 polarization We examined whether PDZ peptide can affect the population of immune cells. Screening of immune cells was performed for immature/mature neutrophils, monocytes, and macrophages in the spleen from the mice by flow cytometry. Although proliferative immature/mature neutrophils were examined after treatment with LPS, the effect of PDZ peptide on an LPS-induced neutrophil lineage was unclear. To investigate this phenomenon, the neutrophil fraction was analyzed with CD11b+Gr1+ in the spleen (Figure 4a). LPS significantly increased the percentage of total neutrophils. The WT PDZ peptide robustly decreased total neutrophils, however, the mut PDZ peptide increased compared to WT PDZ-treated mice (Figure 4a and b). Analyzing total neutrophils in the spleen, there were two populations of neutrophils: a population of CXCR2 +Ly6G+ neutrophils (Mature) and a second population of CXCR2-Ly6Glo/+ neutrophils (immature) (Figure 4c). Both immature and mature neutrophils were dramatically increased by LPS. Importantly, the WT PDZ peptide robustly decreased both immature and mature neutrophils, however, mut PDZ peptide increased them compared to WT PDZ-treated mice (Figure 4d). Next, LPS markedly increased the percentage of CD11b+F4/80int monocytes. There were no differences between the WT PDZ- and mut PDZ-treated mice in the spleen. However, the CD11b+F4/80+ macrophages were dramatically increased in the LPS-treated mice (Figure 4e and f). The WT PDZ peptide robustly decreased macrophages, however, the mut PDZ peptide increased compared to WT PDZ-treated mice (Figure 4e and f). Lastly, to examine whether the PDZ peptide could regulate the M1 and M2 macrophages population and polarization in vivo, spleen cells were stained to characterize the cell populations (Figure 4g). The F480 +CD86+ M1 macrophages were dramatically increased in the LPS-treated mice. The WT PDZ peptide remarkably decreased M1 macrophages, however, mut PDZ peptide increased compared to WT PDZ-treated mice (Figure 4h). The percentage of F4/80+CD206+M2 macrophages were also increased in the LPS-treated mice, however, there were no significant differences between the WT PDZ- and mut PDZ-treated mice (Figure 4i). More importantly, there were no significant differences of the M1/M2 ratio between the LPS- and mut PDZ-treated mice, whereas the ratio was dramatically decreased in WT PDZ-treated mice (Figure 4j). The decrease in the M1/M2 ratio meant that the M2 was relatively increased, suggesting that WT PDZ peptide can inhibit M1 macrophage polarization and promotes M2 macrophage polarization to decrease LPS-induced systemic inflammation. These results show that WT PDZ peptide may inhibit LPS-induced tissue damage and systemic inflammation by regulating the population of immune cells to keep homeostasis during LPS-induced systemic inflammation. ### NF-κB- mediated gene expression levels are downregulated in PDZ peptide-treated cells Although the physiological function of PDZ peptide has become increasingly important in systemic inflammation, the signaling pathway has not yet been fully elucidated. To identify PDZ-mediated signaling, we performed RNA sequencing analysis. The results of RNA-seq analysis showed the expression pattern of 24,424 genes according to each comparison combination, of which the results showed the similarity of 51 genes overlapping in four gene categories and the similarity between each comparison combination (Figure 5a). As a result, compared to the control group, it was confirmed that LPS alone, WT PDZ+LPS, and mut PDZ+LPS were all upregulated above the average value in each gene, and when LPS treatment alone was compared with WT PDZ+LPS, it was confirmed that they were averaged or downregulated. When comparing LPS treatment alone and mut PDZ+LPS, it was confirmed that about half of the genes were upregulated. Regarding the similarity between comparison combinations, the comparison combination with LPS/Control and the comparison combination with WT PDZ+LPS/Control showed the most similar gene patterns, followed by the comparison combination with mut PDZ+LPS/Control. The comparison combination of WT PDZ+LPS/LPS and mut PDZ+LPS/LPS showed similar genetic patterns. Similarity between genes showed that inflammation-related genes had increased expression in the LPS/Control, WT PDZ+LPS/Control, and mut PDZ+LPS/Control treatment groups. NF-kB signaling pathway appeared most frequently in WT PDZ+LPS/LPS (91.46%), Inflammatory autoimmunity appeared most frequently in mut PDZ+LPS/LPS (47.75%), and inflammatory cytokines receptors and inflammasomes also appeared in mut PDZ+LPS/LPS (Figure 5b). It appeared the most at 33.33% and 61.42%. In addition, increased and decreased expression of genes in the inflammatory cytokines receptors gene category was observed in LPS/Control, WT PDZ+LPS/LPS, and mut PDZ+LPS/LPS. Different line thicknesses indicate types of evidence used in predicting the associations. ### PDZ peptide restores LPS-induced mitochondrial dynamics via NF-kB signaling pathway and ROS production in Raw264.7 cells To examine which PDZ peptide affects LPS-induced mitochondrial membrane integrity in Raw 264.7 cells, mitotracker 488 mitochondria dye was utilized. The mitoTracker staining was dramatically decreased in a LPS-time dependent manner (Figure 6a). Interestingly, wild-type PDZ peptide significantly increased the staining compared to LPS only (Figure 6b). These findings suggest that PDZ peptide restored the LPS-induced mitochondrial membrane integrity. However, the mutant PDZ peptide did not have an effect. In addition, the phospho-Drp1 antibody was used to detect LPS-induced mitochondria fission in Raw 264.7 cells. The phospho-Drp1 staining was increased in an LPS-time-dependent manner (Figure 6c). Interestingly, wild-type PDZ peptide significantly decreased the staining compared to LPS only (Figure 6d), suggesting that PDZ peptide can regulate mitochondria fission by controlling phosphorylation of Drp1 to decrease LPS-induced inflammation in Raw264.7 cells. Based on the results of RNA-sequencing analysis (Figure 5), to investigate which signal transduction pathway is induced in the cells stimulated by LPS, LPS was treated in a time-dependent manner. The Western blot analysis was performed using several phospho-specific antibodies (Figure 6e). LPS-induced the phosphorylation of iκB and p65 was significantly peaked at 4 hr and the expression of iNOS by LPS reached a maximum at 30 min and decreased. However, no change in total κB and p65 expressions was observed. Phosphorylation of Drp1 was performed to observe it at the protein level. The phosphorylation of Drp1 by LPS reached a maximum at 4 hr. Interestingly, wild-type PDZ peptide significantly inhibited the expression of iNOS and the phosphorylation of iκB, p65, and Drp1, but not mutant PDZ peptide (Figure 6f), suggesting that NF-κB signaling and ROS production appear to be closely related during PDZ-restored mitochondria dynamics. In addition, we investigated whether wild-type PDZ peptides can alter the expression of specific marker proteins for M1 and M2 polarization. Wild-type PDZ peptide significantly decreased the expression of M1 marker protein (mIL-6, mIL-8, and mTNF-α) (Figure 2b). In addition, the expression of M2 marker protein (mIL-10 and mMRC-1) were increased at 1 hr after the treatment of LPS, but not mFizz-1 (Figure 6g). As opposed to M1 marker proteins, the expression of M2 marker proteins (mIL-10 and mMRC-1) was significantly increased in PDZ-treated cells compared to LPS only, but not mut PDZ peptide (Figure 6h). These results confirmed the observations of the flow cytometry assay performed above (Figure 4h and i). (i) A graphic abstract illustrating that the PDZ peptide of zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) protein inhibits LPS-induced systemic inflammation by regulating the activation of NF-κB signaling pathways, ROS production, and M1/M2 polarization. ## Discussion Systemic inflammation can cause many clinical diseases with high mortality and sepsis-associated organ dysfunction (Dolin et al., 2019). In the present study, we hypothesized that a tight junction protein could affect systemic inflammatory response in LPS-administered mice. The main results are as follows: PDZ peptide administration into LPS-challenged mice significantly decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine production in plasma and BALF and diminished oxidative stress in the kidney; PDZ peptide downregulated immune cell population in spleen cells. Thus, the data indicate the PEGylated PDZ peptide as a therapeutic candidate for LPS-induced acute systemic inflammation. The ZO-1 protein includes protein-protein interaction domains (three PDZ domains) and signaling domains (Hung and Sheng, 2002). In addition, the ZO-1 protein consists of SH3 and catalytically inactive GuK domains. In our previous studies (Lee et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2020), the PDZ peptide strongly inhibited LPS- or PM2.5-induced airway inflammation in the mice respiratory tract. The physiological functions identified were as follows: PDZ peptide strongly suppressed LPS- or PM2.5-induced F-actin polymerization to result in decreased airway inflammation. Also, expression of CXCR2 as the receptor for IL-8 secretion activated by LPS was significantly inhibited by PDZ, whereas RGS12 expression that has a GTPase-activating function increased after PDZ peptide treatment and downregulated CXCR2 receptor activation. However, these phenomena were confined to only the respiratory tract. We could not determine whether ZO-1 is involved in LPS-induced systemic inflammation or if the PDZ peptide could downregulate systemic inflammation. Therefore, we are currently investigating the physiological symptoms of systemic inflammation caused by LPS in ZO-1 conditional knock-out mice. In the present study, the PEGylated PDZ peptide was considered an innovative therapeutic candidate to decrease LPS-induced systemic inflammation in mice. However, although colistin has poor efficacy and renal toxicity, it is a powerful antibiotic used as a last resort to treat infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria (Sabnis et al., 2021). In addition, treatment failure occurs frequently, and the efficacy of colistin is very low (Paul et al., 2018; MacNair et al., 2018; Satlin et al., 2020). Furthermore, colistin has significant renal and neurological side effects that generate oxidative stress (Spapen et al., 2011). However, the PDZ peptide in the present study did not have any side-effects and decreased ROS generation in renal mitochondria (Figure 3). Nevertheless, the physiological mechanisms by which the PDZ peptide can control LPS-induced systemic inflammation in mice and the signal molecules involved, especially in the downstream signaling of G-protein, remain unclear. Hypothetically, because PDZ has a TAT sequence as a cell-penetrating peptide (CPP), the peptide easily enters the mitochondria to regulate ROS generation. The PDZ peptide inhibited iNOS and eNOS activities in human bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2B; data not shown), but the mut PDZ peptide did not. In our previous studies (Lee et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2020; Kim and Song, 2022), LPS secreted many cytokines and/or chemokines extracellularly to signaling pathways associated with inflammation to nearby cells, inducing severe cytokine storm in several organs. However, the PDZ peptide strongly inhibited these extracellular secretions at the cellular level. Because the PDZ domain can bind to many signaling-related proteins through PDZ-PDZ interactions (Lee and Zheng, 2010; Lee et al., 2006; Gisler et al., 2008), the signaling complex might regulate systemic inflammation. To investigate PDZ-binding partners in mammalian cells, the GST:PDZ complex was immunoprecipitated from BEAS-2B cells transfected with the construct. The binding proteins are currently being identified using tandem mass spectrometry analysis. Neutrophils dominate the initial stage of inflammation by pathogen invasion, and macrophages are activated and differentiated by receiving signals from the microenvironment of damaged tissues, which are coordinated by the expression of numerous cytokines and receptors (Butterfield et al., 2006). Therefore, neutrophils and macrophages perform various roles, such as the defense of the body from pathogens, regulation of the inflammatory environment, tissue development, homeostasis, etc., and are therapeutic targets related to a wide range of inflammation. The spleen functions as a unique extramedullary reservoir for myeloid cells, including monocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils. Recently, Deniset et al. revealed the existence of two distinct neutrophil populations within the red pulp (RP) of the spleen: the mature Ly6Ghigh neutrophils, and the immature Ly6Gint neutrophils (Deniset et al., 2017). Therefore, in the present study, the relationship between PDZ peptide and two distinct neutrophil populations was investigated in the spleen. The percentage and number of total neutrophils dramatically increased by LPS treatment were significantly decreased by WT PDZ peptide, but mut PDZ peptide increased them compared to the WT PDZ peptide. These results, also, were the same in the analysis of immature and mature neutrophils. Interestingly, the proportion of immature neutrophils was much higher than that of mature neutrophils during LPS-induced systemic inflammation (Figure 4). These were similar to the results found by Deniset et al. That is, after infection with Streptococcus pneumonia, Ly6Ghigh mature neutrophils within the RP of the spleen were replenished by Ly6Gint immature neutrophils. This phenomenon was thought to be due to the local increase of Ly6Gint immature neutrophils as a consequence of an extramedullary hematopoiesis and their differentiation into Ly6Ghigh mature neutrophils (Deniset et al., 2017). Although the WT PDZ peptide did not reduce the increased monocytes caused by LPS-induced inflammation, it dramatically decreased the percentage and number of macrophages (Figure 4). In particular, the WT PDZ peptide dramatically reduced the M1 macrophages increased by LPS and significantly decreased the M1/M2 ratio, thereby promoting the M2 polarization of macrophages (Figure 4). The results indicated that the proinflammatory microenvironment of the LPS challenge might increase M1 macrophage polarization by inflammatory cytokines and/or chemokines inhibiting M2 macrophage polarization. However, the WT PDZ peptide treatment significantly inhibited M1 polarization to activate M2 polarization. Therefore, the results of the present study demonstrate an innovative therapeutic candidate for an increased ratio of M2 macrophages in the immune cell population during LPS-induced systemic inflammation. In addition, the PDZ peptide can alter the immature/mature neutrophil ratio and population of immune cells. Recently, mitochondria have an important role in the control of inflammatory responses (Marchi et al., 2023). In addition, mitochondria have emerged as being necessary for both the establishment and maintenance of innate and adaptive immune cell responses (Sandhir et al., 2017; Weinberg et al., 2015). Thus, we focused on the key function of mitochondria in regulating the innate immune response and the mitochondrial dysfunction known to be promoted by inflammation, we investigated whether mitochondria that modulate inflammatory signaling are regulated by PDZ peptides. LPS-induced mitochondrial membrane integrity and fission are critical in the inflammatory response, and we showed that PDZ regulates LPS-induced systemic inflammation by modulating these phenomena. ROS induced by potassium deprivation increased the phosphorylation of Drp1 to mitochondrial fragmentation (Cid-Castro and Morán, 2021). Although more precise studies are needed, the inhibition of iNOS expression by PDZ peptide inhibited ROS formation (Figures 3e and 6f). (3) The phosphorylation of Drp1 has been known to be critical for mitochondria fission (Xie et al., 2020). ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.95285.4.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.95285.4.sa1)

Summary:

The authors investigated systemic inflammation induced by LPS in various tissues and also examined immune cells of the mice using tight junction protein-based PDZ peptide. They explored the mechanism of anti-systemic inflammatory action of PDZ peptides, which enhanced M1/M2 polarization and induced the proliferation of M2 macrophages. Additionally, they insisted the physiological mechanism that inhibited the production of ROS in mitochondria, thereby preventing systemic inflammation.

Strengths:

In the absence of specific treatments for septic shock or sepsis, the study demonstrating that tight junction-based PDZ peptides inhibit systemic inflammation caused by LPS is highly commendable. Whereas previous research focused on antibiotics, this study proves that modifying parts of intracellular proteins can significantly suppress symptoms caused by septic shock. The authors expanded the study of localized inflammation caused by LPS or PM2.5 in the respiratory tract to systemic inflammation, presenting promising results. They not only elucidated the physiological mechanism by identifying the transcriptome through RNA sequencing but also demonstrated that PDZ peptides inhibit the production of ROS in mitochondria and prevent mitochondrial fission. This research is highly regarded as an excellent study with potential as a treatment for septic shock or sepsis.

Weaknesses:

(1) They Focused intensively on acute inflammation for a short duration instead of chronic inflammation.

(2) LPS was used to induce septic shock but administrating actual microbes such as E. coli would yield more accurate results.

(3) The authors used pegylated peptides, but future research should utilize the optimized peptides to derive the optimal peptide, and further, PK/PD studies are also necessary.

results.result: PEGylated PDZ peptide was successfully synthesized and characterized. The PDZ peptide consists of 22 amino acids with a TAT sequence for cell permeability and was tagged with FITC. PEGylation using m-PEG-succinimidyl succinate (MW 5000 Da) yielded mono- and di-PEGylated products that were successfully separated by size exclusion chromatography and confirmed by SDS-PAGE analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C47 describe the peptide design and PEGylation process with supporting data from Figure 1. The chromatography and gel electrophoresis data provide clear evidence of successful PEGylation at lysine residues, resulting in increased hydrodynamic volume. The methodology is well-documented and the results are consistent with the stated objectives.

results.result: WT PDZ peptide treatment improved survival and reduced plasma biomarkers in LPS-challenged mice. WT PDZ-treated mice showed decreased levels of ALT, AST, BUN, and creatinine compared to LPS-only treated mice, with significant effects on creatinine levels. Survival was significantly increased with WT PDZ pretreatment but not with mutant PDZ peptide.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C54 are supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 2a showing biochemical markers and survival curves. The use of mutant PDZ as a negative control strengthens the conclusion that the effects are sequence-specific. However, sample sizes (n=5) are relatively small for survival studies, and statistical significance indicators are present but p-values are not explicitly stated in the table.

results.result: WT PDZ peptide significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production in plasma and lung BALF. IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α levels were significantly decreased in WT PDZ-treated mice but not in mutant PDZ-treated mice, maintaining homeostasis in blood and lungs after LPS administration.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C55, C57, C58 are well-supported by ELISA data in Figure 2b and 2c. The consistent pattern across multiple cytokines and both plasma and BALF samples strengthens the conclusion. The inclusion of mutant PDZ controls demonstrates specificity. Statistical significance is indicated, though the exact p-values and multiple testing corrections are not fully detailed.

results.result: WT PDZ peptide restored LPS-induced tissue injuries in liver, kidney, and lung. Histological analysis showed that inflammatory cell infiltration was significantly inhibited by WT PDZ administration but not mutant PDZ. Iba1 staining for macrophages/microglia was dramatically decreased in liver and kidney with WT PDZ treatment, and PAS-positive goblet cells in lung tissue were reduced.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C59-C66 are supported by comprehensive histological data in Figure 3a-c with semi-quantitative analysis in Figure 3d-f. The use of multiple staining methods (H&E, Iba1, PAS) across multiple organs provides robust evidence. The mutant PDZ control demonstrates specificity. However, the semi-quantitative analysis methods could be better described, and blinding of evaluators is not mentioned.

results.result: WT PDZ peptide protected against LPS-induced kidney cell toxicity and blocked ROS production in renal mitochondria. MTT assay showed that WT PDZ significantly alleviated LPS-induced cell damage, while mutant PDZ did not. ROS production in kidney mitochondria increased in a time-dependent manner with LPS, but was blocked by WT PDZ peptide.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71, C11, C35 are supported by MTT assay (Figure 3g) and ROS measurement data (Figure 3h). The time-course data for ROS production strengthens the mechanistic interpretation. However, the claim that PDZ inhibits systemic inflammation specifically by hindering ROS production in kidney mitochondria (C35) is somewhat overstated, as ROS reduction is only one of multiple mechanisms demonstrated.

results.result: WT PDZ peptide reduced total, immature, and mature neutrophil populations in the spleen. Flow cytometry revealed two distinct neutrophil populations (CXCR2+Ly6G+ mature and CXCR2-Ly6Glo/+ immature), both dramatically increased by LPS. WT PDZ robustly decreased both populations, while mutant PDZ increased them compared to WT PDZ-treated mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C73-C77 are well-supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4a-d. The identification of distinct neutrophil populations and differential effects of WT vs mutant PDZ provide strong evidence. The proportion of immature neutrophils being higher than mature (C148) is an interesting observation consistent with extramedullary hematopoiesis during inflammation.

results.result: WT PDZ peptide selectively reduced macrophage populations without affecting monocytes. While LPS increased both monocytes and macrophages, WT PDZ dramatically decreased macrophages but did not reduce monocytes. Mutant PDZ increased macrophages compared to WT PDZ-treated mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81, C151-C152 are supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4e-f. The selective effect on macrophages but not monocytes is an important mechanistic distinction. However, the biological significance of this differential effect could be better explained, particularly regarding the maturation pathway from monocytes to macrophages.

results.result: WT PDZ peptide shifted macrophage polarization from M1 to M2 phenotype. M1 macrophages (F4/80+CD86+) were dramatically increased by LPS and remarkably decreased by WT PDZ. While M2 macrophages (F4/80+CD206+) showed no significant difference between WT and mutant PDZ treatment, the M1/M2 ratio was dramatically decreased in WT PDZ-treated mice, indicating promotion of M2 polarization.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C87, C153, C155 are strongly supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4g-j. The M1/M2 ratio analysis (Figure 4j) is particularly compelling evidence for the polarization shift. However, the interpretation that M2 was 'relatively increased' (C87) based on ratio changes rather than absolute numbers should be noted. The mechanism by which PDZ promotes M2 polarization remains incompletely explained.

results.result: RNA sequencing analysis identified NF-κB signaling as the dominant pathway affected by PDZ peptide. Among 51 overlapping inflammation-related genes, NF-κB signaling pathway appeared most frequently in WT PDZ+LPS/LPS comparison (91.46%). Protein-protein interaction analysis showed strong interactions between NF-κB, mTOR, REL, SAA1, and CXCL3.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C90-C99 are supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 5. The heatmap, gene category analysis, and STRING database results provide convergent evidence for NF-κB pathway involvement. However, the RNA-seq was performed on BEAS-2B cells (human bronchial epithelial), not the mouse model used for other experiments, which limits direct mechanistic interpretation. The fold-change and normalization methods are described but statistical thresholds for significance could be clearer.

results.result: WT PDZ peptide restored LPS-induced mitochondrial membrane integrity in Raw264.7 cells. MitoTracker staining decreased in an LPS-time-dependent manner, but WT PDZ significantly increased staining compared to LPS alone. Mutant PDZ had no effect on mitochondrial membrane integrity.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C100-C103 are supported by MitoTracker staining data in Figure 6a-b. The time-course experiment and comparison with mutant PDZ strengthen the conclusion. However, MitoTracker staining reflects both mitochondrial mass and membrane potential, so the specific claim about 'membrane integrity' could be more precisely stated. Additional assays (e.g., JC-1 for membrane potential) would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: WT PDZ peptide decreased LPS-induced mitochondrial fission by reducing Drp1 phosphorylation. Phospho-Drp1 staining increased in an LPS-time-dependent manner but was significantly decreased by WT PDZ treatment. This suggests PDZ regulates mitochondrial fission by controlling Drp1 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C104-C106 are supported by phospho-Drp1 staining (Figure 6c-d) and Western blot data (Figure 6e-f). The time-course and specificity to WT PDZ strengthen the conclusion. However, the causal link between reduced Drp1 phosphorylation and decreased inflammation (C106) is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. Experiments with Drp1 inhibitors or mutants would strengthen this mechanistic claim.

results.result: WT PDZ peptide inhibited LPS-induced NF-κB signaling pathway activation. Western blot analysis showed that phosphorylation of IκB and p65 peaked at 4 hours, iNOS expression peaked at 30 minutes, and Drp1 phosphorylation peaked at 4 hours after LPS treatment. WT PDZ significantly inhibited these phosphorylation events and iNOS expression, but mutant PDZ did not.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C107-C111, C164 are well-supported by comprehensive Western blot time-course data in Figure 6e-f. The temporal dynamics of different pathway components and the specificity to WT PDZ provide strong mechanistic evidence. However, quantification of Western blots is not shown, and loading controls appear consistent but densitometry analysis would strengthen the claims.

results.result: WT PDZ peptide modulated M1 and M2 macrophage marker expression. WT PDZ significantly decreased M1 marker proteins (mIL-6, mIL-8, mTNF-α) and increased M2 marker proteins (mIL-10, mMRC-1) compared to LPS treatment alone. Mutant PDZ did not produce these effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13, C113-C115 are supported by qPCR data in Figure 6g-h. The results are consistent with the flow cytometry data on M1/M2 polarization (Figure 4), providing convergent evidence. However, the claim references Figure 2b for C113, which appears to be an error as Figure 2b shows plasma cytokines, not macrophage marker gene expression. This inconsistency should be noted.

results.result: PDZ peptide regulates mitochondrial dynamics through coordinated effects on NF-κB signaling and ROS production. The inhibition of NF-κB signaling by PDZ affects mitochondrial dynamics, representing a novel finding. PDZ inhibits iNOS expression, reducing ROS formation, which in turn decreases Drp1 phosphorylation and mitochondrial fission, ultimately suppressing LPS-induced systemic inflammation.
results.evaluation: Claims C112, C116, C163, C166, C169, C171-C172 integrate multiple experimental findings into a mechanistic model. The evidence from Western blots (Figure 6e-f), mitochondrial staining (Figure 6a-d), and ROS measurements (Figure 3h) support this integrated mechanism. However, the causal relationships are largely inferred from correlative data. The claim of novelty (C166) regarding PDZ inhibition of NF-κB affecting mitochondrial dynamics is reasonable but would benefit from more direct mechanistic experiments (e.g., NF-κB inhibitors, genetic manipulations).

results.result: PEGylated PDZ peptide is proposed as a therapeutic candidate for LPS-induced systemic inflammation. The peptide inhibits systemic inflammation by reducing tissue injuries, preventing biochemical marker alterations, decreasing pro-inflammatory cytokine production, reducing oxidative stress, and regulating immune cell populations to maintain homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15, C38, C72, C88, C118-C120, C156, C175 represent the overall therapeutic conclusion. While the experimental data supporting anti-inflammatory effects are strong, the designation as a 'therapeutic candidate' is speculative. Key limitations include: (1) only prophylactic (pretreatment) administration was tested, not therapeutic (post-LPS) treatment; (2) only acute inflammation (5 days) was examined; (3) no pharmacokinetic or toxicity data are provided; (4) translation from mouse to human is uncertain; (5) the mechanism of action, while partially elucidated, remains incomplete. These claims require substantial additional validation before therapeutic candidacy can be established.

results.result: Background context establishes that LPS-induced systemic inflammation is a significant clinical problem with limited treatment options, and that ZO-1 protein and its PDZ domain have previously shown anti-inflammatory effects in respiratory inflammation, but effects on systemic inflammation were unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C16-C27 provide background context supported by appropriate citations. These establish the rationale for the study. The claims about prior PDZ peptide effects (C22-C26) cite the authors' own previous work, which is appropriate. The identification of the research gap (C27) is reasonable and well-motivated.

results.result: Background on macrophage polarization and neutrophil populations establishes that M1/M2 macrophage balance and immature/mature neutrophil populations are important determinants of inflammatory responses, and that the spleen serves as a reservoir for these immune cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C34, C143-C147 provide immunological background supported by appropriate citations. This context is essential for interpreting the flow cytometry results. The information about neutrophil populations in the spleen (C147) from Deniset et al. is particularly relevant to the experimental findings.

results.result: PEGylation rationale and comparison to colistin establishes that peptide therapeutics require half-life extension, and that current treatments like colistin have significant limitations including renal toxicity and poor efficacy, while PDZ peptide showed no side effects and decreased ROS in renal mitochondria.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43, C129-C133 provide rationale for PEGylation and context for therapeutic potential. The comparison to colistin is supported by citations. However, the claim that PDZ peptide 'did not have any side-effects' (C133) is overstated—the study did not comprehensively assess toxicity, only showed lack of obvious adverse effects in the acute model and demonstrated reduced ROS. Formal toxicity studies would be needed to support this claim.

results.result: Literature context on sepsis, organ damage, ROS, and mitochondrial dynamics establishes that ZO-1 has been identified as a sepsis marker, that systemic inflammation causes multi-organ damage, that ROS production is a key mechanism of LPS toxicity, and that mitochondrial dynamics and NF-κB signaling are interconnected in inflammatory responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C56, C69, C117, C160-C161, C165, C168, C170 provide relevant mechanistic background supported by appropriate citations. This context helps interpret the experimental findings regarding mitochondrial function and NF-κB signaling.

results.result: Acknowledged limitations and future directions include incomplete understanding of signaling pathways, ongoing studies with ZO-1 knockout mice, unclear downstream G-protein signaling, hypothesized mechanisms of mitochondrial entry, unpublished data on iNOS/eNOS inhibition, and speculation about anti-inflammatory cytokine production and broader disease applications.
results.evaluation: Claims C89, C127-C128, C134-C137, C141-C142, C158-C159, C174 appropriately acknowledge limitations and propose future work. The hypothesis about TAT-mediated mitochondrial entry (C135) is reasonable but speculative. The mention of unpublished data (C136-C137) is noted but cannot be evaluated. The speculative statements about mechanisms (C141, C158) and future applications (C159, C174) are appropriately qualified.

results.result: Discussion of prior findings and mechanistic interpretations includes ZO-1 structure, previous PDZ peptide effects on respiratory inflammation, mechanisms involving F-actin and CXCR2/RGS12, neutrophil population dynamics, macrophage polarization mechanisms, and the relationship between tissue injury and immune cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C126, C138-C140, C148-C150, C154, C157, C162, C167, C173 integrate prior findings with current results. The discussion appropriately cites previous work and makes reasonable mechanistic interpretations. However, some mechanistic claims (e.g., C154 about proinflammatory microenvironment effects) are inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The comparison to Deniset et al. findings (C148-C150) provides useful context for the neutrophil data.

results.result: The authors successfully synthesized and characterized PEGylated PDZ peptides (both wild-type and mutant) using size exclusion chromatography and SDS-PAGE analysis, demonstrating that PEGylation was achieved through amine-coupling at lysine residues and substantially increased the hydrodynamic volume of the peptides.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the PEGylation methodology or characterization. The editor noted that 'results from cellular and in vivo experiments tracking key inflammatory markers are compelling,' implicitly accepting the foundational peptide preparation work.

results.result: PDZ peptide administration restored LPS-induced tissue injuries in kidney, liver, and lung, prevented alterations in biochemical plasma markers (ALT, AST, BUN, creatinine), reduced inflammatory cell infiltration, decreased Iba1 staining in liver and kidney, reduced PAS-positive goblet cells in lung, and alleviated kidney cell toxicity.
results.evaluation: The editor stated that 'results from cellular and in vivo experiments tracking key inflammatory markers are compelling.' The reviewer praised the study as 'highly commendable' and noted that the authors 'presented promising results' regarding tissue protection. No concerns were raised about the histological or biochemical data.

results.result: Wild-type PDZ peptide significantly increased survival, decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α) in plasma and lung BALF, and maintained homeostasis in blood and lungs after LPS administration, while mutant PDZ peptide showed no such effects.
results.evaluation: The editor described the results as 'compelling' and the reviewer noted the study 'proves that modifying parts of intracellular proteins can significantly suppress symptoms caused by septic shock.' The survival and cytokine data were not questioned by reviewers.

results.result: PDZ peptide significantly inhibited inflammation by decreasing populations of M1 macrophages and neutrophils (both immature and mature), increasing M2 macrophages, and decreasing the M1/M2 ratio, thereby regulating immune cell populations to maintain homeostasis during LPS-induced systemic inflammation.
results.evaluation: The reviewer specifically praised the work, stating 'They explored the mechanism of anti-systemic inflammatory action of PDZ peptides, which enhanced M1/M2 polarization and induced the proliferation of M2 macrophages.' The editor found the inflammatory marker tracking 'compelling.' No concerns were raised about the flow cytometry data or immune cell analysis.

results.result: RNA sequencing analysis revealed that NF-κB-related protein expression was lower in PDZ-treated cells than in LPS-treated cells, with NF-κB signaling pathway appearing most frequently (91.46%) in the WT PDZ+LPS/LPS comparison, suggesting NF-κB signaling dominates the anti-inflammatory effects of PDZ peptide.
results.evaluation: The reviewer commended the authors for elucidating 'the physiological mechanism by identifying the transcriptome through RNA sequencing.' The editor did not raise concerns about the RNA-seq analysis. The mechanistic insights were viewed positively as part of the overall compelling evidence.

results.result: Wild-type PDZ peptide significantly increased mitochondrial membrane integrity (MitoTracker staining) and decreased LPS-induced mitochondria fission (phospho-Drp1 staining), suggesting PDZ peptide can regulate mitochondria fission by controlling phosphorylation of Drp1.
results.evaluation: The reviewer specifically highlighted that the authors 'demonstrated that PDZ peptides inhibit the production of ROS in mitochondria and prevent mitochondrial fission.' The editor found the results 'compelling.' No methodological concerns were raised about the mitochondrial studies.

results.result: PDZ peptide dramatically reduced LPS-induced NF-κB signaling, ROS production, expression of M1 macrophage markers, and increased M2 macrophage markers, while inhibiting iNOS expression and phosphorylation of iκB, p65, and Drp1, thereby regulating mitochondrial membrane integrity and dynamics to suppress systemic inflammation.
results.evaluation: The reviewer praised the mechanistic work, stating the authors 'insisted the physiological mechanism that inhibited the production of ROS in mitochondria, thereby preventing systemic inflammation.' The editor found the cellular and in vivo experiments 'compelling.' No concerns were raised about the Western blot, qPCR, or ROS measurement data.

results.result: PEGylated PDZ peptide inhibits LPS-induced systemic inflammation, reduces tissue injuries, reestablishes homeostasis, and may be an innovative therapeutic candidate for sepsis, septic shock, and systemic inflammation including human pulmonary diseases.
results.evaluation: While the editor stated the work 'provides a proof of concept for developing novel strategies against acute inflammatory conditions such as sepsis,' the reviewer noted weaknesses including that the study 'focused intensively on acute inflammation for a short duration instead of chronic inflammation' and that 'LPS was used to induce septic shock but administrating actual microbes such as E. coli would yield more accurate results.' The therapeutic potential is acknowledged but with caveats about model limitations.

results.result: This is the first study to show that inhibition of NF-κB signaling by PDZ affected mitochondrial dynamics.
results.evaluation: The reviewer described the research as 'highly regarded as an excellent study with potential as a treatment for septic shock or sepsis' and praised the mechanistic insights. The novelty claim was not challenged by reviewers, and the editor characterized the study as 'important.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on PEGylation methodology and characterization (C39-C47). Both evaluations find the peptide design and preparation well-supported. OpenEval provides detailed technical assessment while peer reviewers implicitly accepted this foundational work without raising concerns.

Complete agreement on RNA-seq data supporting NF-κB pathway involvement (C7, C90-C99). Both find the transcriptomic analysis compelling. OpenEval notes the limitation of using human BEAS-2B cells rather than mouse cells, which peer reviewers did not explicitly address.

Strong agreement on cytokine reduction data (C5, C55, C57-C58). Both evaluations find ELISA results compelling. OpenEval notes small sample sizes and requests explicit p-values, while peer reviewers found results 'compelling' without raising statistical concerns. Peer review also includes survival claims C53-C54.

Partial overlap on survival and biochemical markers (C48-C51, C53-C54). Both find the data supported. OpenEval specifically notes small sample sizes (n=5) and lack of explicit p-values, concerns not raised by peer reviewers who found the survival data compelling.

Strong agreement on histological evidence of tissue protection (C3, C59-C66). Both evaluations find the multi-organ, multi-staining approach compelling. OpenEval requests better description of semi-quantitative methods and blinding procedures, which peer reviewers did not address. Peer review encompasses broader tissue protection claims including C4, C67-C68.

Partial overlap on cellular viability and ROS data (C67-C68, C70-C71, C11, C35). Both find MTT and ROS measurements supportive. OpenEval cautions that C35 overstates ROS as the sole mechanism. Peer reviewers grouped these with broader tissue protection findings without noting mechanistic overstatement.

Complete agreement on neutrophil population data (C6, C73-C77). Both find flow cytometry evidence compelling. OpenEval notes the interesting observation about immature vs mature neutrophils (C148), while peer reviewers praised the immune cell analysis without detailed technical commentary.

Strong agreement on macrophage vs monocyte differential effects (C78-C81, C151-C152). Both evaluations support the findings. OpenEval requests better explanation of biological significance, while peer reviewers incorporated this into broader praise of immune cell polarization work.

Complete agreement on M1/M2 macrophage polarization (C82-C87, C153, C155). Both find the flow cytometry data compelling. OpenEval notes that M2 increase is relative rather than absolute and requests mechanistic explanation. Peer reviewers specifically praised the M1/M2 polarization findings as a key contribution.

Strong agreement on mitochondrial membrane integrity data (C8, C100-C103). Both find MitoTracker staining supportive. OpenEval notes the assay reflects both mass and membrane potential, suggesting JC-1 assays would strengthen claims. Peer reviewers found mitochondrial studies compelling without requesting additional assays.

Agreement on Drp1 phosphorylation and mitochondrial fission (C9, C104-C106). Both evaluations support the findings. OpenEval notes the causal link to inflammation is inferred rather than demonstrated and suggests Drp1 inhibitor experiments. Peer reviewers praised the mitochondrial fission prevention without noting inferential limitations.

Strong agreement on Western blot time-course data for signaling pathways (C10, C107-C111, C164). Both find the temporal dynamics compelling. OpenEval requests densitometry quantification, while peer reviewers found the mechanistic evidence compelling without requesting quantification.

Agreement on qPCR data for macrophage markers (C12-C13, C113-C115). Both find results consistent with flow cytometry. OpenEval identifies a figure reference error (C113 cites Figure 2b incorrectly). Peer reviewers did not note this discrepancy.

Agreement on integrated mechanistic model (C112, C116, C163, C166, C169, C171-C172). Both support the NF-κB/mitochondrial dynamics mechanism. OpenEval notes causal relationships are largely correlative and requests direct mechanistic experiments. Peer reviewers praised the physiological mechanism elucidation without requesting additional causal validation.

Agreement on novelty claim (C166). Both evaluations support the novel mechanistic insights regarding PDZ inhibition of NF-κB affecting mitochondrial dynamics. OpenEval qualifies this as reasonable but needing more direct experiments, while peer reviewers described the research as 'highly regarded' and 'excellent.'

Significant disagreement on therapeutic candidacy claims (C14-C15, C38, C72, C120, C156, C175).
